import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):

        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)

        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom

        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

            "Parity bits detect if an error occurred.",
            "Even parity makes the total count of ones even.",
            "However, it cannot locate or fix the error."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title_text, lecture_lines)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Show binary "101" (#FFFFFF); a green '0' (#00FF00) appears at the end.

        bit1 = Text("1", font_size=48, color="#FFFFFF")
        bit2 = Text("0", font_size=48, color="#FFFFFF")
        bit3 = Text("1", font_size=48, color="#FFFFFF")
        
        # Fix Issue 33: Shift bits left
        self.place_at_grid(bit1, "C1")
        self.place_at_grid(bit2, "C2")
        self.place_at_grid(bit3, "C3")
        
        data_bits = VGroup(bit1, bit2, bit3)
        
        # Fix Issue 33: Shift parity bit left
        parity_bit = Text("0", font_size=48, color="#00FF00")
        self.place_at_grid(parity_bit, "C4")
        
        # Fix Issue 33: Shift parity label left
        parity_label = Text("Parity Bit", font_size=24, color="#00FF00")
        self.place_at_grid(parity_label, "B4", scale_factor=0.7)
        
        self.play(Write(data_bits))
        self.play(FadeIn(parity_bit), FadeIn(parity_label))
        self.wait(2)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===

        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FFFF00")

            ReplacementTransform(bit2, error_bit),
            bit1.animate.set_color("#FF0000"),
            bit3.animate.set_color("#FF0000"),
            parity_bit.animate.set_color("#FF0000"),
            parity_label.animate.set_color("#FF0000")
        )

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # === Setup Layout ===
        title_text = "The Power of 2: Positioning Bits"
        lecture_lines = [
            "Parity bits occupy positions at powers of two.",
            "All other positions hold the actual message data.",
            "This specific layout enables the mathematical correction magic."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title_text, lecture_lines)

        # Define indices for parity and data
        parity_indices = [0, 1, 3]  # Positions 1, 2, 4 (0-indexed)
        data_indices = [2, 4, 5, 6]    # Positions 3, 5, 6, 7 (0-indexed)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Description: Display numbers 1-7; highlight 1, 2, and 4 in blue (#5555FF). Change Line 1 color to #FFFF00. self.wait(2).
        
        # Highlight lecture line first
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#FFFF00"))
        
        # Create slots and numbers
        slots = VGroup(*[
            Circle(radius=0.4, color="#FFFFFF").set_stroke(width=2) 
            for _ in range(7)
        ]).arrange(RIGHT, buff=0.3)
        
        nums = VGroup(*[
            Text(str(i), font_size=24, color="#FFFFFF") 
            for i in range(1, 8)
        ])
        for n, s in zip(nums, slots):
            n.move_to(s.get_center())
            
        bit_positions = VGroup(slots, nums)
        # Using Area C1-C6 as suggested by VideoCritic (Issues 38 & 39)
        self.place_in_area(bit_positions, "C1", "C6", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        self.play(FadeIn(bit_positions))
        self.wait(0.5)

        # Highlight powers of 2 (positions 1, 2, 4)
        self.play(
            *[slots[i].animate.set_color("#5555FF") for i in parity_indices],
            *[nums[i].animate.set_color("#5555FF") for i in parity_indices],
            *[Indicate(nums[i], color="#5555FF") for i in parity_indices]
        )
        self.wait(2.0)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Description: Fill positions 3, 5, 6, 7 with white 'D' characters (#FFFFFF). Change Line 2 color to #FFFF00. self.wait(2).
        
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#FFFF00"))
        
        d_labels = VGroup()
        for i in data_indices:
            d = Text("D", font_size=24, color="#FFFFFF")
            d.move_to(slots[i].get_center())
            d_labels.add(d)

        # Morph numbers at positions 3, 5, 6, 7 to 'D' labels
        self.play(
            *[Transform(nums[i], d_labels[idx]) for idx, i in enumerate(data_indices)]
        )
        self.wait(2.0)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Description: Arrange the labels into the sequence [P1, P2, D3, P4, D5, D6, D7]. Change Line 3 color to #FFFF00. self.wait(2).
        
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#FFFF00"))
        
        # Define final labels for the sequence
        # Index map: 0:P1, 1:P2, 2:D3, 3:P4, 4:D5, 5:D6, 6:D7
        final_label_texts = ["P1", "P2", "D3", "P4", "D5", "D6", "D7"]
        final_colors = ["#5555FF", "#5555FF", "#FFFFFF", "#5555FF", "#FFFFFF", "#FFFFFF", "#FFFFFF"]
        
        final_labels = VGroup()
        for i in range(7):
            lbl = Text(final_label_texts[i], font_size=22, color=final_colors[i])
            lbl.move_to(slots[i].get_center())
            final_labels.add(lbl)

        # Transform current elements into the full [P, D] sequence
        transforms = []
        # Transform parity numbers (already blue) to P1, P2, P4
        for i in parity_indices:
            transforms.append(Transform(nums[i], final_labels[i]))
        
        # Transform current 'D' characters to D3, D5, D6, D7

outline.topic: Error Correction and Hamming Codes: The Self-Healing Data
outline.target_audience: University students (Computer Science or Electrical Engineering)

sections.title: The Problem: The Noisy Universe
sections.content: Introduce the concept of data corruption during transmission. Explain that in the real world, cosmic rays, electromagnetic interference, or hardware glitches can flip a '0' to a '1'. Show that without a check system, the receiver has no way of knowing the data is wrong.
sections.example: Astro the Robot sends the binary message '1011' (representing 'Turn Left') to a Mars Rover. Due to space radiation, the Rover receives '1001' ('Turn Right'), causing a potential collision.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Simple Parity Bit
sections.content: Introduce the simplest form of error detection: Parity. Explain 'Even Parity' where we add a single bit to make the total count of 1s even. Highlight the limitation: it can detect that an error happened, but it can't tell you *where* it happened or how to fix it.
sections.example: Data '101' has two 1s. We add a parity bit '0' to keep it even (1010). If the Rover receives '1110', it sees three 1s and knows there's an error, but doesn't know which bit flipped.

sections.title: The Hamming Logic: Overlapping Circles
sections.content: Introduce Richard Hamming’s breakthrough using a visual Venn Diagram of three overlapping circles (A, B, C). Place data bits in the intersections and parity bits in the outer segments of each circle. Explain that every data bit is 'watched' by multiple parity bits.
sections.example: Visualize 3 circles labeled P1, P2, and P3. A data bit 'd1' sits where all three circles overlap. If 'd1' flips, all three parity bits will report an error, pointing uniquely to that specific intersection.

sections.title: The Power of 2: Positioning Bits
sections.content: Transition from circles to a linear sequence. Explain the rule: Parity bits are placed at positions that are powers of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8...). All other positions are for data. This binary indexing is the key to the 'math magic' of Hamming Codes.
sections.example: For a 7-bit message: Positions 1, 2, and 4 are Parity (P). Positions 3, 5, 6, and 7 are Data (D). The sequence looks like: [P1, P2, D3, P4, D5, D6, D7].

sections.title: The Calculation: Who Checks Whom?
sections.content: Explain how to determine which parity bit covers which data bit using binary addresses. Parity bit 1 (binary 001) checks all positions with a '1' in the rightmost bit. Parity bit 2 (010) checks positions with a '1' in the middle bit, etc. Use an animation to highlight these binary patterns.
sections.example: P1 (001) checks positions 1, 3, 5, 7. P2 (010) checks positions 2, 3, 6, 7. This creates a unique 'fingerprint' for every bit position.

sections.title: Correction: Finding the 'Syndrome'
sections.content: Demonstrate the 'Syndrome' calculation. When data is received, we re-calculate the parity bits. If the checks fail, we add the position numbers of the failing parity bits. The sum is the exact index of the flipped bit.
sections.example: If Parity checks P1 and P2 fail but P4 passes, we add their positions: 1 + 2 = 3. Position 3 is the error! We flip bit 3 back to its original state, and the data is perfectly restored.

sections.title: Real-World Impact: From RAM to Deep Space
sections.content: Conclude by showing where this is used today. Explain that ECC (Error Correction Code) RAM in servers uses Hamming codes to prevent system crashes, and space probes use advanced versions to talk to Earth across millions of miles.
sections.example: Show a server motherboard. Explain that without Hamming codes, your bank's computer might flip a bit in your balance, turning $1,000 into $0.

storyboard.title: The Power of 2: Positioning Bits
lecture_lines: Parity bits occupy positions at powers of two.
All other positions hold the actual message data.
This specific layout enables the mathematical correction magic.

storyboard.title: The Calculation: Who Checks Whom?
lecture_lines: Every bit position has a unique binary address.
Parity bit 1 checks addresses ending in one.
Parity bit 2 checks addresses with a middle one.
Parity bit 4 checks addresses starting with one.
This creates a digital fingerprint for every position.
animations: List binary indices 001 to 111 vertically in white (#FFFFFF). Change Line 1 color to #FFFF00. self.wait(2).
Highlight rows with a '1' in the last digit in cyan (#00FFFF) with label "Checks P1" (#00FFFF). Change Line 2 color to #FFFF00. self.wait(2).

Highlight index 011 (3) to show it's within both cyan and magenta groups. Change Line 5 color to #FFFF00. self.wait(2).

storyboard.title: Correction: Finding the 'Syndrome'
lecture_lines: Recalculate each parity bit in the received message.
Red indicators show which parity checks failed.
Sum the positions of the failing parity bits.
This sum identifies the exact error location.
Flip the identified bit to correct the data.
animations: Show the bit sequence [P1, P2, D3, P4, D5, D6, D7] in white (#FFFFFF). Highlight parity bits P1, P2, P4 as they are recalculated. Change Line 1 color to #FFFF00. self.wait(2).
P1 and P2 turn red (#FF0000), indicating they fail their parity checks. Label "FAIL" (#FF0000) appears above them. Change Line 2 color to #FFFF00. self.wait(2).

The bit at position 3 (D3) is highlighted with a yellow box (#FFFF00) and label "ERROR BIT" (#FFFF00). Change Line 4 color to #FFFF00. self.wait(2).

storyboard.title: Real-World Impact: From RAM to Deep Space
lecture_lines: Hamming codes protect modern server memory from crashes.
They allow deep-space probes to communicate reliably.
This math ensures your bank balance remains accurate.
